lead: Adsorption takes a solute out of a gas or a liquid by holding it on the surface of a porous solid. The solid is the adsorbent, the held solute is the adsorbate, and nearly all of the surface lies inside the pores. Plants use it to decolourise sugar syrup, polish drinking water, recover solvent vapour, dry air and split oxygen from air. How much an adsorbent can hold depends on its surface area, its pore sizes and the force that holds the molecules.

blocks.text: A molecule at a solid surface has neighbours on one side only, so the surface attracts molecules from the fluid that touches it. When a solute molecule is held there, it has been adsorbed. Absorption is different: in gas absorption the solute dissolves into the whole body of a liquid. Adsorption stays at the surface, even though that surface is mostly the walls of pores inside each grain. When both may happen, or the mechanism is unclear, the general word is sorption.

Adsorption releases heat, the heat of adsorption, because held molecules have less energy than free ones. Two consequences follow for the plant. A bed warms as it loads, which lowers its capacity and in solvent recovery can even start a fire in a carbon bed. And a loaded adsorbent gives up its solute when it is heated or when the pressure is dropped, which is how it is regenerated and reused.

The solute reaches a site in three steps in series: across the stagnant film of fluid around the grain, along the pores into the grain, and onto the surface itself. The first two set how fast a bed works; the equilibrium of the last step sets how much it can hold.

Syllabi ask for the two types of adsorption side by side. Physical adsorption (van der Waals adsorption) uses the same weak forces that condense a vapour. Chemisorption forms a chemical bond between the adsorbate and the surface.

blocks.text: Nearly all separation adsorbers rely on physical adsorption, because the adsorbent must be regenerated thousands of times. Chemisorption is the first step of heterogeneous catalysis.

Capacity is measured as the loading q, the mass of adsorbate held per unit mass of dry adsorbent, often mg/g or kg/kg. More surface means more sites, so good adsorbents are made highly porous. One gram of activated carbon can expose 1000 m² of surface, about four tennis courts. Pores are sorted by width: micropores below 2 nm, mesopores 2–50 nm and macropores above 50 nm.

Micropores give most of the area, and their opposite walls overlap their pull, so they hold small molecules strongly. They are also slow to enter and may be too narrow for large dye or protein molecules. Macropores add little area but act as roads that carry the fluid quickly into the grain. A good adsorbent has both: macropores and mesopores feeding the micropores. The particle size matters too: small grains are loaded faster, but they raise the pressure drop through a bed.

blocks.where: Batch test: W of dry adsorbent shaken with volume V of solution until the concentration stops changing. C<sub>0</sub> and C<sub>e</sub> are the initial and equilibrium concentrations; solute lost by the liquid is gained by the solid. With C in mg/L, V in L and W in g, q is in mg/g.

Typical use

blocks.text: Polar adsorbents (silica gel, alumina, zeolites) prefer water and other polar molecules; non-polar carbon prefers organic molecules and works in wet streams. Zeolites are named by pore opening: 3A (about 0.3 nm) admits water but not ethanol, so it dries ethanol; 4A and 5A admit larger molecules; 13X is the widest. A zeolite separates nitrogen from oxygen by equilibrium, not size: both molecules enter, but nitrogen's larger electric quadrupole is held more strongly by the cations in the cages, so oxygen leaves first and the product is oxygen-rich. A carbon molecular sieve works the other way, by rate: the slightly smaller oxygen molecule diffuses in faster, so a short cycle gives nitrogen-rich product.
Ion-exchange resins look like adsorbents (porous beads in a column) but work by swapping ions of equal charge, as described in Ion exchange principles and equipment.

examples.question: 2.00 g of activated carbon is shaken with 100 mL of a dye solution of 50 mg/L until equilibrium; the liquid then holds 10 mg/L. (a) Find the loading q and the fraction of dye removed. (b) Assuming q stays the same at the same final concentration, how much carbon treats 1000 L of the same solution to 10 mg/L?
steps: Volume in litres: V = 100 mL = 0.100 L.
q = 4.0 mg/2.00 g = 2.0 mg/g. Fraction removed = 40/50 = 80 %.
(b) Dye to remove from 1000 L = 40 mg/L × 1000 L = 40 000 mg.
Carbon = 40 000/2.0 = 20 000 g = 20 kg. Batch contact uses the loading in equilibrium with the final, lowest concentration, so the carbon is used at only 2.0 mg/g.
examples.answer: q = 2.0 mg/g, 80 % of the dye removed; 20 kg of carbon treats 1000 L in one batch.

examples.question: An activated carbon has a surface area of 1000 m²/g. A benzene molecule lying flat covers about 0.40 nm². Estimate the benzene held by 1 g of carbon if one complete layer covers the whole surface (benzene 78.11 g/mol).
steps: Area of one molecule = 0.40 nm² = 0.40 × 10<sup>−18</sup> m².
Mass = 4.15 × 10<sup>−3</sup> × 78.11 = 0.324 g, so q ≈ 324 mg/g, about one third of the carbon's own mass.
examples.answer: A monolayer holds about 0.32 g of benzene per g of carbon, which is why area is the first figure quoted for an adsorbent.

traps: Adsorption is not absorption: the solute stays on the pore walls of the solid; in absorption it dissolves into the whole liquid.
Using V = 100 with mg/L gives 4000 mg instead of 4.0 mg. Convert mL to L.
q is mass of solute per mass of dry adsorbent, not a concentration in the liquid.
Physical adsorption falls as temperature rises because it is exothermic; that is the basis of regeneration by heating.
A zeolite does not split O<sub>2</sub> from N<sub>2</sub> by sieving size: both enter, and N<sub>2</sub> is held more strongly. The carbon molecular sieve is the one that separates by rate.

quiz.a: The adsorbent is the porous solid that holds the solute on its surface; the adsorbate is the solute held there.

quiz.q: Give the size ranges of micropores, mesopores and macropores.
quiz.a: Micropores below 2 nm, mesopores 2–50 nm, macropores above 50 nm.

quiz.q: Give four differences between physical adsorption and chemisorption.
quiz.a: Physical adsorption uses van der Waals forces, has a low heat (20–40 kJ/mol), is non-specific, can form several layers and is easily reversed. Chemisorption forms a bond, has a high heat (80–400 kJ/mol), is specific, stops at one layer and is often hard to reverse.

quiz.q: 5.00 g of carbon is shaken with 250 mL of solution; C<sub>0</sub> = 80 mg/L and C<sub>e</sub> = 20 mg/L. Find q.
Why does a good adsorbent need macropores as well as micropores?
quiz.a: Micropores give the area and strong holding but are slow to enter; macropores carry the fluid quickly into the grain so the micropores are reached in a useful time.

quiz.q: A zeolite bed and a carbon molecular sieve bed are both fed with air. Which product gas does each give, and why?
quiz.a: The zeolite holds N<sub>2</sub> more strongly (its quadrupole interacts with the cations), so it delivers O<sub>2</sub>-rich gas: an equilibrium separation. The carbon molecular sieve lets O<sub>2</sub> diffuse in faster, so in a short cycle it holds O<sub>2</sub> and delivers N<sub>2</sub>-rich gas: a rate separation.

quiz.q: Name the adsorbent you would choose to dry ethanol, and say why.
quiz.a: Zeolite 3A: its opening of about 0.3 nm admits water but not the larger ethanol molecule, and as a polar solid it holds water strongly.

beyond: Not for the exam. The surface area quoted for an adsorbent is measured by nitrogen adsorption at −196 °C and the BET equation; the pore size spread comes from the same data. Newer adsorbents include metal–organic frameworks, whose pores can be designed molecule by molecule, and biochar made from farm waste. Search for BET surface area, metal–organic framework and biochar adsorbent.

The boxes give the chapter's worked examples: a batch test giving q = 2.0 mg/g, the 20 kg of carbon needed for 1000 L, and the monolayer estimate for 1000 m²/g.
